Evidence: The component list gives die counts only (5 black, 4 blue, 2 orange, 4 green). No section of the manuscript states the faces of any die; the Introduction promises a standalone rulebook. Faces reconstructed from DS-Extended-Rules-V45 p.27 card images, Core p.12 and V2 p.25 examples (see B_report §1).
Proposed fix: Add after the dice list: "Each die shows the following faces. Black: 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2. Blue: 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3. Orange: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4. Green (dodge): three blank faces and three faces showing one dodge symbol." Also correct "2X Orange" to "2x Orange".
Rationale: A standalone rulebook must define the randomisers it uses; every balance figure in this audit depends on these faces. The listed sets are the only sorted six-face sets consistent with all supplied evidence; the author must confirm against the physical dice.
Gameplay impact: None if confirmed; if the author's dice differ, every probability in B_report must be re-run.

Evidence: Defence total = two highest dice. With black dice the ceiling is 4 (2+2); mean of 2 black = 2.33, best-two-of-3 black = 2.88, best-two-of-4 black = 3.19. Official 1E (Core p.25) sums all dice (3 black mean 3.50). Combined with the Enemy Scaling table (L1519) this caps what any block build can absorb.
Current text: Determine the defence total by adding the number of sword pips on the highest two dice results. Additional dice beyond the two with the highest shown face value are ignored.
Proposed fix: Keep the rule but state the consequence in the Enemy Scaling section (see B-003/B-004) or raise the cap: "Determine the defence total by adding the number of sword pips on the highest two dice results. A shield adds its block dice to the pool and, if the character has a shield equipped, the three highest dice are used instead."
Rationale: Hollowed Edition p.7 introduced the two-dice cap to tame armour stacking, but it was paired with unscaled enemy attack values. The manuscript adds +1 attack at 3 players and Repeat at 4 players against the same cap, so damage leaks through on every hit at 3-4 players.
Gameplay impact: At 4 players a scaled Hollow Soldier (attack 5, Repeat 2) deals an expected 5.3 damage per activation to a 2-black-die blocker (see §2).

Evidence: Hollow Soldier (Core p.20: attack 4). At 4 characters: attack 5 with Repeat 2. Expected damage per activation vs 2 black block dice (best two) = 2 x 2.67 = 5.33 of an 8-box bar; P(kill full-health character in one activation) = 0.058; P(kill hollow character) = 0.444. At 1-2 characters the same enemy deals 1.67. Official 1E (Core pp.17-25) and V2 (p.16, player-count symbol = extra models) never add attack value or Repeat.
Current text: If playing with four characters, add *repeat to* each non-boss enemy's attack behaviour. [table: 4 | Base + 3 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | Repeat 2]
Proposed fix: Delete the Repeat row. Replace with: "If playing with four characters, increase each non-boss enemy's base health by one further point (Base + 4)." Table row 4: "4 | Base + 4 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | -".
Rationale: Repeat doubles damage on top of the +1; with the two-highest-dice block cap no build can absorb it. A health step keeps the 4-player encounter longer without making single activations lethal.
Gameplay impact: 4-player expected damage per Hollow Soldier activation falls from 5.33 to 2.67; one-activation kill chance on a full bar falls from 5.8% to 0%.

Evidence: +1 attack at 3 characters raises Hollow Soldier expected damage from 1.67 to 2.67 (+60%) and removes the zero-damage block outcome (P(0) 0.111 -> 0). The health step (+1) is a +33% change at the same player count. Three characters also absorb three times the enemy activations of one character because all enemies act between every character turn (L1297-1311).
Current text: If playing with three or more characters, increase all non-boss attack values by one. [table: 3 | Base + 2 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | -]
Proposed fix: "If playing with four characters, increase all non-boss enemy attack values by one." Table: row 3 "3 | Base + 2 | 1 -> 2 | - | -"; row 4 "4 | Base + 3 | 1 -> 2 | +1 | -".
Rationale: Moves the attack step to the player count where the party has the most defensive redundancy and keeps each step of the table roughly equal in expected-damage terms.
Gameplay impact: 3-player encounters return to 1-2 player per-hit lethality while keeping +2 health per enemy.

Evidence: Skeleton Soldier (V2 p.24) has no attack icon; its only damage is a push attack inside its move. The rule adds Repeat to the 'attack behaviour'; it is undefined whether a push-move with damage counts, and the 2-player move 1 -> 2 rule already doubles that enemy's possible hits.
Current text: If playing with four characters, add *repeat to* each non-boss enemy's attack behaviour.
Proposed fix: If Repeat is retained: "Repeat applies to attack icons only. Movement behaviours, including push-moves that deal damage, are never repeated."
Rationale: Removes an ambiguity that otherwise quadruples push-mover damage at 4 players (two moves x Repeat 2).
Gameplay impact: Prevents a 2-damage push enemy becoming an 8-hit threat.

Location: L1511 vs L1523 (Enemy Data Cards vs Enemy Scaling)
Evidence: L1511 says scaled health = base + one per character 'in play'; L1523 says base + characters 'beyond one'. For 1 character these give base+1 and base respectively; the table (row 1 'Base Health') agrees with L1523.
Current text: When playing with more than one character, calculate a scaled health value by adding one health for each character (including dead characters) in play.
Proposed fix: "When playing with more than one character, calculate a scaled health value by adding one health for each character (including dead characters) beyond the first."
Rationale: Makes the two statements and the table agree.
Gameplay impact: Removes a one-health discrepancy at every player count.

Evidence: Tier Three 8 and Tier Four 8 are equal; every other cost progression is strictly increasing. The campaign table (L2303-2306) is exactly double the basic row for Tiers One-Three (4/8/16) and gives Tier Four 20, implying basic Tier Four = 10. Cumulative basic cost one stat: 2/6/14/22 as written, 2/6/14/24 with 10.
Rationale: Preserves the author's own 1:2:4:5 ratio between the basic and campaign tables; 16 (doubling) would cost 30 cumulative, 68% of a character's whole-game income (44 souls), and would never be bought.
Gameplay impact: Tier Four costs 24 cumulative (55% of basic income) instead of 22; reaching it remains a deliberate end-game choice.

Location: L1391 (Souls) and Soul Reward Table L1401-1434
Evidence: "reward the reduced soul reward" is used but no reduced value appears anywhere in the manuscript. Candidate values: half rounded down 1/2/2/3 (re-clear of four tiles = 6-8 souls), half rounded up 2/2/3/3, reward-2 1/2/3/4 (campaign L1 would be 0), flat 1.
Current text: Upon successfully *clearing* an encounter that has been previously *cleared*, reward the reduced *soul* reward to each character.
Proposed fix: "Upon clearing an encounter that has previously been cleared, each character gains half the listed soul reward, rounded down." Add a third column to both Soul Reward Tables headed "Reduced reward": basic 1 / 2 / 2 / 3; campaign 1 / 1 / 2 / 2.
Rationale: Half-rounded-down is the strongest anti-grind value that still pays; a full four-tile re-clear (6-8 souls) is worth less than one Tier Three step (8), which matches the stated design goal of removing grinding.
Gameplay impact: Defines a rule that currently cannot be played; caps repeat income at about +14 souls per game.

Location: L1393 and L1415-1424 (Souls; Soul Reward Table row labels)
Evidence: L1393 says invaders give 'additional souls per player' without a number; the only figures are the row labels 'Standard Invaders 3' and 'Advanced Invaders 4' inside the encounter table. Official 1E gives 3 souls to the shared cache for any invader (Phantoms p.15), i.e. 0.75 per character at 4 players; the manuscript gives 3-4 per character, 4-5x the official reward.
Current text: Successfully defeated invaders provide additional *souls* per player.
Proposed fix: "A defeated standard invader provides three souls to each character; a defeated advanced invader provides four souls to each character, in addition to the encounter reward."
Rationale: States the figure in prose where the rule lives; the table alone is not a rule.
Gameplay impact: Confirms an invader is worth a whole extra encounter per character; acceptable given invaders act after every character turn (L2027).

Evidence: Solo start 6 souls (from Hollowed Edition p.2). Official 1E solo bonus is 16 souls in the cache (Core p.13) because one character carries every activation. Under the manuscript's unscaled 1-character enemies 6 souls = three tier-one cards or Tier One in three stats.
Current text: Characters adventuring alone start with six *souls* on their dashboard.
Proposed fix: No change required; if solo play tests as too hard, raise to ten souls.
Rationale: The reduced solo bonus is consistent with the manuscript's scaling (solo enemies are weakest).

Location: L2301-2306 with L2247-2280 (Campaign Stat Tier Costs and Campaign Soul Reward Table)
Evidence: First Journey (Core p.35 structure) under the campaign table yields about 55 souls per character over three sections; one stat to Tier Three costs 28 (51% of all income), Tier Four 48 (87%), four stats to Tier Three 112 (204%). The campaign both halves the per-encounter reward relative to level (2/3/4/5 vs 3/4/5/6) and doubles level costs.
Current text: | Tier Three | **16** | / | Tier Four | **20** | (campaign) and campaign rewards 2/3/4/5
Proposed fix: Keep the campaign reward table at the basic values (3 / 4 / 5 / 6) and retain the doubled stat costs; or keep 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 and set campaign Tier Three to 12 and Tier Four to 16.
Rationale: Two simultaneous halvings make a three-session campaign end with most characters at Tier Two in one stat, below where the basic game ends after one session; one lever is enough to slow progression.
Gameplay impact: With basic rewards the campaign total rises to about 73 per character: one stat to Tier Three plus a second to Tier Two plus two tier-two cards, i.e. one full tier beyond the basic game across three sessions.

Location: L1197 (Objective & Loss Conditions) with L1223 and L1341 (forced rest)
Evidence: A failed encounter 'forces' the party to spend one spark and rest. The loss condition only triggers when all characters are dead and no sparks remain. The state 'hollow character dies, survivors standing, spark dial at 0' is undefined: the forced rest cannot be paid. Spark budgets: 4 players have three paid rests in the whole basic game.
Current text: The players lose collectively if at any point, all characters are dead and there are no remaining sparks to revive them.
Proposed fix: "The players lose the game when an encounter is failed and the spark dial shows zero."
Rationale: A failed encounter always demands a spark; defining the loss at that moment closes the gap and matches official 1E (Core p.8: once the dial reads 0, the next time a character is killed the game is lost).
Gameplay impact: Makes the end state deterministic; no numeric change.

Evidence: Campaign maximum = starting sparks (4 players: 2). A boss defeated at a full dial gives nothing. Adding a fourth player to a three-player party holding 1 spark leaves 0 sparks with a maximum of 2. Official 1E campaign (Core p.33) allowed buying a spark for 2 souls per character up to the maximum; the manuscript forbids any purchase.
Current text: The starting number of sparks also serves as the maximum number of sparks. ... Sparks cannot be purchased or gained otherwise. ... New players can join a campaign that is in progress at the cost of one spark each.
Proposed fix: "The maximum number of sparks is the starting number plus one. While resting at the bonfire the characters may buy one spark for four souls per character, up to the maximum. A new player may join only while the spark dial shows at least two."
Rationale: Restores the official pressure valve at double the official price (consistent with the manuscript's doubled prices) and removes the two degenerate states.
Gameplay impact: A four-player campaign can hold up to 3 sparks and can convert about 16 souls into a rest when a section goes badly.
